newsitem.title: UK: EURO OIL SWAPS MOSTLY DIP BUT BRENT CFDS STAY FLAT.
newsitem.headline: EURO OIL SWAPS MOSTLY DIP BUT BRENT CFDS STAY FLAT.

text.p: European oil swaps slipped on Monday, extending losses seen towards the end of last week.
Brent futures were flat despite the imminent resumption of Iraqi oil sales which loom over the market.
Iraq is due to sell its first oil for nearly three months over the next couple of days and plans an export rush of 1.5 million barrels per day during August.
Despite that prospect wet Brent cargoes were unchanged, as were CFDs which remain stubbornly in contango.
This week's dates talked 38 cents under October with the following three weeks at 34 cents, 33 cents and 33 cents under October respectively.
The middle distillates swaps market endured an extremely quiet day of activity, with values for EN590 broadly unchanged but 0.2 percent diesel and jet values were seen slipping marginally.

Trades of the day were concentrated in the jet market, which saw a third quarter 1998 trade at a $24.00 premium to gas oil and rumours of October trades in the $22.25-$22.75 range and of a fourth quarter trade in the prevailing $224.75-$225.25 range.
Brokers and banks placed EN590 values at $6-$7 for September, around $8 for October, $9-$9.50 for November and $9-$10 for fourth quarter.

Gas oil cracks were meanwhile talked by brokers at $4.45 for fourth quarter, well down from fairly recent offers as high as $4.60, while first quarter 1998 was values at $4.40 and second quarter at $4.00.

Gasoline crack talk was virtually non-existent as September outrights were heard traded at $192 and $192.25 as levels slipped by $1-$2 on the day on lower crude futures and a $6 -$7 decline in cash levels.
Naphtha swaps were fairly active for September, which saw trades at $185.25, $185.50, $185.75 and $186, according to brokers.
By late afternoon, August swaps were seen $1 up on the day at $190-$191 as September/October were seen flat at $185-$186, barely changed against the open.
Heavy fuel swaps fell $1 a tonne but activity was slow. High sulphur barges talked $93.50 for August and September but were pegged nearer $100 for January and February.
"It was a slow day. There bits and pieces traded but there was no real trend," said a broker. -- Sam Arnold-Forster, London Newsroom +44 171 542 4984
